narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the model estimates that you have a 61.8 percent chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt if you were admitted. That is a high risk, and the university decided this outweighed the potential for success.

The single most important factor driving this prediction was your academic standing in your third year of study. You belong to the second decile of your class, meaning you are near the bottom compared to accepted students, who typically sit around the sixth decile. This low ranking is a strong signal that your academic performance is not on track for the rigorous demands of law school and the bar exam.

The second most influential factor worked in your favor. Your LSAT score, though slightly below the average of accepted students, actually pushed the prediction toward passing. This suggests your standardized test performance gave the model some reassurance about your aptitude. However, it was not enough to overcome the serious concerns raised by your academic record.

The third factor, your first-year class decile, also pushed toward failure. Being in the third decile in Year 1—far below the accepted average of six—indicates that struggles began early and continued. Together, your low class rankings across multiple years convinced the model that the risk of bar failure is high.

To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your grades through post-baccalaureate coursework, retake the LSAT to strengthen your application, and consider seeking academic support to demonstrate sustained improvement. These steps could shift the balance in your favor next time.
